newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia denies freezing ties with Singapore.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia denies freezing ties with Singapore.

text.p: Malaysia declared on Thursday it had not frozen ties with neighbouring Singapore, denying reports that threatened to plunge relations between the Southeast Asian neighbours to their lowest level in 30 years.
At the heart of the sudden new flareup were remarks by Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew about the Malaysian state of Johor which he retracted when it caused a row a month ago.
"No decision has been made to freeze ties with Singapore as reported by the local newspapers," acting Foreign Minister Abang Abu Bakar Abang Mustapha said in a statement on Thursday.

Although the Malaysian cabinet discussed ties between the countries, "I would like to stress that whatever has been reported by the mass media as their main subject in the leading local newspapers today (Thursday) are not accurate," he said.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad, visiting Tokyo, told a news conference he was not fully briefed on what exact action his cabinet took.
"I would like to know more about this before I explain the reason why. They must have had some reason for making this decision. But I don't think this is a major problem," he said.

The national news agency Bernama and Malaysian newspapers quoted unidentified ministers as saying after Wednesday's cabinet meeting that fresh initiatives with Singapore would be suspended, including new contracts to Singaporean companies.

Bernama also quoted Culture, Arts and Tourism Minister Sabbaruddin Chik as saying all bilateral meetings would be postponed indefinitely. The decision would cover all fresh dealings or those being planned for implementation on a government-to-government level, it said.

Bernama quoted Information Minister Mohamed Rahmat as saying Malaysia did not want to be "over-enthusiastic" in forging ties with Singapore. He said Singapore should not treat the matter as easily solved merely because Lee apologised.
The original row erupted after Lee, in a court affidavit leaked to the Malaysian press, described the southern state of Johor as a place "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".

Lee apologised and instructed his lawyer to ask the court to delete the remarks, made in a deposition in a libel suit against a Singaporean opposition politician who fled to Johor after saying he had received death threats in Singapore.

Works Minister S. Samy Vellu told reporters on Thursday the cabinet only decided to suspend a culture and sports agreement with Singapore. "We did not discuss anything about relationships or anything," he said.

The ringgit and Singapore dollar fell sharply on Thursday over the reports, dealers and analysts said. The Singapore dollar fell to an 18-month low and the Malaysian ringgit's steady rise against the dollar was halted.
"The market just reacted to Malaysia's decision. People sold both Sing dollar and ringgit," said a dealer with a European bank in Singapore.
Singapore reacted with stunned dismay on Thursday to the latest flare-up.

"I think I want to take some time to understand Malaysia's reaction before I comment," Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong told reporters after talks with visiting Australian Prime Minister John Howard.
"I want to absorb the implications of all this before I give my comments," Goh said.
During a visit to Laos earlier this week, Goh had said it was time for Singapore and Malaysia "to move on" after Malaysia accepted Lee's "unreserved apology".
"There is a Malay saying that water cannot be separated, even with a knife. This is the nature of our relations with Malaysia," he was quoted as saying in Laos by Singapore media.
